claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: structured product issuant go from approximately 500 billion globally to a trillion dollars per year of structured product issu
claims.claim: Global structured product issuance doubled in two years to about USD 1 trillion a year, adding to volatility supply.
claims.direction: more vol supply, lower implied vol

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the structur product issuance I believe is a secular Trend that is not going away
claims.claim: Structured-product issuance is a secular trend, so index vol supply and low correlation should persist into 2025, while the liquidity driver is less reliable.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: around that time where where a lot of empires start to um to have you know not always right but question marks
claims.claim: Around the 250-year mark empires tend to face a critical juncture, layered on top of the shorter fourth-turning cycle, and the US is at one now.
claims.testable: no - single historical analogy, no defined signal

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Nothing, literally nothing, is more important than positioning itself.
claims.claim: Positioning is the only reliable driver of outcomes because the net effect of who is long or short outweighs news (Soros reflexivity).

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: if the world is long, the odds are are much higher, right, that it will go down. And if the world is short, the odds are much higher that it will go up.
claims.claim: Crowded long positioning raises odds of a decline and crowded short positioning raises odds of a rally (contrarian positioning signal).
claims.conditions: not a certainty, a tailwind or headwind to the outcome
claims.testable: yes - positioning extremes vs forward returns

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: markets go up 20% in two months like they just did. That's $50 trillion of collateral.
claims.claim: Because equity markets are now so large (a 20% move is about $50T of collateral), positioning flows outweigh the effect of small liquidity changes or geopolitical news.
claims.testable: partly - market size vs flow impact

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: everybody thought they were positioned for something that was obvious and inevitable. So, once again, the opposite happened.
claims.claim: When everyone positions for an obvious outcome (oil spike on a Middle East war), the opposite tends to happen.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: capex is driving everything but it's capex um that's not a very laborheavy capex right
claims.claim: The economy is K-shaped: AI infrastructure capex drives growth but is not labor-heavy, so jobs numbers soften while the capex-linked market stays strong.
claims.direction: soft labor data alongside strong equities

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Earnings growth is 100% coming from that capex build and and it's a reflexive loop.
claims.claim: Index earnings growth comes entirely from the AI capex build, a reflexive loop where the market itself, not the broad economy, drives outcomes.
claims.indicator: S&P earnings growth contribution from AI capex

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: earnings last quarter was from the increased value of anthropic
claims.claim: A large share of one mega-cap's reported earnings came from mark-ups of its AI-lab stake rather than customer demand, showing earnings are inflated by capital-market valuations (speaker misnames the stake).
claims.indicator: mark-to-market gains on AI stakes in earnings

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: there was no real money to be made from a longfall trade
claims.claim: Long-vol hedges earned nothing in the Q1 2026 drawdown (about 9-10%) because the decline was slow and grinding, and the fast rebound then hurt them.
claims.direction: long vol payoff low in slow declines
claims.conditions: slow decline followed by fast V-recovery
claims.testable: yes - vol-strategy returns by drawdown speed

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: hedging and using long vvall uh is always frustrating
claims.claim: Systematic long-vol hedging is chronically frustrating because it pays only in sudden moves, and hedges have repeatedly failed (2022, April 2025, 2026).
claims.testable: yes - long-vol carry cost vs payoff

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: callvall is inordinately cheap
claims.claim: Call volatility is cheap relative to the larger, faster upside moves now occurring (e.g. 50% in two months in hyperscalers), so right-tail convexity pays, especially with dispersion.
claims.indicator: call skew / call implied vol vs realised upside
claims.testable: yes - call vol vs realised upside moves

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: it's the more convex outcome and that can be right tail and left tail
claims.claim: Volatility strategies are the distribution of all outcomes and the convex bet that can win from either tail; right-tail players did well in 2026.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: socialism/communism with with American characteristics
claims.claim: The US is adopting state-directed capitalism (government stakes, picking winners), analogous to China's capitalism with Chinese characteristics, because great-power competition forces it.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: once America starts moving and start makes a decision move aggressively. That's when regimes at least the last 250 years begin to change aggressively
claims.claim: The US reacts late to crises but once it decides to act it moves aggressively, and that is when regimes change; accumulated pressures are now forcing action.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Unsustainable debt, populism which we've talked about at uh at length.
claims.claim: First pressures forcing regime change are unsustainable debt and populism, both accelerating.
claims.testable: partly - debt/GDP measurable, populism is not

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: baby boomers are dying and over the next decade we're going to hit you know a even greater populist impulse
claims.claim: Populism is accelerating as baby boomers die (examples: billionaire tax, proposals for 50% state ownership of AI firms) and becomes accepted on both sides.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: structural inflation which is not going away and if anything um accelerating
claims.claim: Structural inflation persists and accelerates due to global conflict, protectionism, fiscal spending and populism.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: cannot we can no longer allow a twoarter decline of more than 20%
claims.claim: The equity market is too big to fail: a two-quarter decline above 20% would drain liquidity and growth too much, so policy will not tolerate it.
claims.testable: partly - frequency of >20% two-quarter declines under the thesis

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: an intractable conflict with China to decide who is going to make the rules of the next 40, 50, 100 years
claims.claim: The US-China fight over who holds the primary reserve currency and sets the rules is the fifth pressure pushing for state action.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: they are going to create a sovereign wealth fund that buys within the next decade 10 to 15 trillion dollars of equities and they're going to do it by printing money
claims.claim: The US will back-stop the Treasury market and fund a sovereign wealth fund buying $10-15T of equities via money creation, using the dollar's exorbitant privilege.
claims.direction: long US equities, short purchasing power

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Japan owns 8 to 9% of the DK. It's already been done before.
claims.claim: Precedent: Japan's central bank owns 8-9% of its equity market and Norway runs a ~$3T sovereign wealth fund, so state equity ownership via money creation has been done.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: printing money cannot happen in England or Turkey or Zimbabwe because they don't have natural structural demand for the currency
claims.claim: Only a reserve-currency issuer can print money at scale without a currency collapse, so the US can do what weaker countries cannot.
claims.conditions: only for currencies with structural demand

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: This is the fifth stake they've taken in a company.
claims.claim: The US government is taking equity stakes in firms (Intel 10%, others, OpenAI 5% offered), and Karsan expects stakes to rise to 10-20% each and then broaden into trillions.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: I believe it's in the next year. I think it's before June of next year
claims.claim: A moment is coming (before June 2027) when the government buys massive stakes across a broad swath of businesses worth over a trillion dollars, trillions within a year or two.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: you are essentially instead of taxing the rich and giving it to the poor in a traditional way, you are taxing the rich by simply taking stakes in those equity businesses
claims.claim: A state-funded equity fund short-circuits the populism of a K-shaped economy by giving everyone ownership instead of taxing the rich directly.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the only way you get rid of the debt is through monetizing it anyway
claims.claim: The plan supports equities, competes with China and short-circuits populism but drives massive inflation, which is intended because monetization is the only exit from the debt.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: that market goes up that drives more investment in US businesses which drives growth
claims.claim: Government equity buying lifts the market (Intel rose about 40% on the stake), raising investment and growth, with proceeds going to the Treasury to back-stop social programs.
claims.testable: yes - event study of government stake announcements

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: greatest risk is that China quite frankly doesn't want the US to do this
claims.claim: The plan is not fair globally and the main risk is China (and the rest of the world) pushing back.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: after the midterms and before June in a meaningful way
claims.claim: Large-scale government equity buying will start after the Nov 2026 midterms and before June 2027, aiming to get markets moving ahead of the 2028 election.
claims.direction: long equities from post-midterm to mid-2027

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: feature not a bug that they keep taking it down to take it up again
claims.claim: The administration deliberately lets markets fall and then reverses to rally them, so expect repeated drop-then-rally cycles.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Iran and Venezuela and Panama and Philippines are all about. They are creating a moat.
claims.claim: US actions in Iran, Venezuela, Panama and the Philippines aim to build a moat around dollar-denominated trade (commodities priced in dollars) against Chinese yuan trade.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: there's this period November to June where again uh you should expect um full throttle re-engagement
claims.claim: The Iran deal holds only until the midterms; expect full re-engagement and renewed oil/commodity volatility from November to June.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the US wants to control trade as much as it can and it wants to make sure most importantly that trade is continues to be done in dollars
claims.claim: The US will not accept Iranian or Chinese control or taxation of Hormuz traffic in other currencies, so conflict continues beyond the nuclear justification.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: The administration also needs to and will in my opinion move more to the center.
claims.claim: After the midterms the administration will move to the centre by linking markets to populism (Trump and Sanders converging), which unifies both sides behind the plan.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: we'll probably get a pretty ugly November to June
claims.claim: The risk is infighting over who gets what; a crisis is what unites people, hence a messy November to June.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: They have a implicit if not explicit wink wink nod nod keep going we got your back
claims.claim: AI hyperscalers borrow to fund huge capex because of an implicit government backstop (buying their stock, bailing them out), and not playing along risks punishment.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: capex is different this time because there's an implicit guarantee the US government's going to keep driving that cap.
claims.claim: The AI capex cycle differs from the dot-com bubble because the US government implicitly guarantees it to compete with China.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: we are definitely in a bubble without um the investment and the promises and the control of the most big bully dominant force in the world
claims.claim: Valuations are a bubble that only holds because of government support (Fed, Treasury); without it the outcome is bad, so the question is whether they retain control.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: there's less control now and that means more risk.
claims.claim: The US waited 10-20 years to act, so the plan has less control and more risk, with China likely to poke at it (gray swans).

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: this is the don't fight the Fed thing, but on steroids with the whole US system
claims.claim: With the whole US system (Treasury, Fed, government stakes) behind the market, do not bet against it in the short to medium term.
claims.testable: partly - 'don't fight the Fed' as a rule

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: will things mean revert? Um in a natural system, yes.
claims.claim: Mean reversion applies in a natural market, but a state-managed market is probably not natural, so valuation-based reversion is less reliable.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: You need someone at the head of the Fed that at least appears and can initially act as if they are independent
claims.claim: Warsh is the good cop appearing independent to protect dollar credibility while Bessent is the bad cop pushing printing and stock buying; Fed independence is shrinking.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the Federal Reserve will hop on and begin to backs stop
claims.claim: Sequence: the Treasury buys back its own debt first, then in a crisis the Fed backstops the long end of the curve.
claims.direction: long-end yields capped in a crisis

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: they're also not doing what the Japanese central bank did, which is just buy stocks themselves
claims.claim: The plan routes equity purchases through a Treasury sovereign wealth fund funded by borrowing and printing, not direct central-bank stock buying, because it looks fairer.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: volumes drop in half yet compre structured products stay the same
claims.claim: Summer of George: in summer, volumes halve while structured-product hedging stays constant, compressing volatility further.
claims.testable: yes - seasonality of vol and volume

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: whatever they're long tends to go down and whatever uh people are short tends to go up and you get massive dispersion
claims.claim: In compressed summer markets, hedge funds' long positions fall and shorts rise, producing large dispersion.
claims.direction: short crowded longs, long crowded shorts

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: if you have all compression at the index level, that tends to mean if something goes up, something else has to go down.
claims.claim: Index vol compression forces the net to zero, so single-name moves are offsetting and correlations break down in summer.
claims.testable: yes - implied correlation index vs dispersion

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: in that process you should do the opposite
claims.claim: In the summer-of-George regime, do the opposite of recent winners (fade momentum/positioning), and expect it for roughly the next month.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: There's three majors. There's flows.
claims.claim: Framework: short/medium-term markets are driven by three legs: flows (structural, including summer, year-end, midterm), macro (rates, inflation, growth) and the administration itself.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: flex structural flows are very positive until let's say September
claims.claim: Flows are positive until about September while macro is slowly degrading, so expect choppy but no negative fireworks; markets can also support macro via a reflexive loop.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: populist periods, elections matter more than ever
claims.claim: Election outcomes matter more in populist periods and especially this midterm, since losing both houses would stop the plan, so the administration will do all it can to hold the Senate.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: a two-month period where the flows are less positive, but the administration is very intent to keep it going
claims.claim: September to early November is a more volatile window: flows fade, macro worsens, administration pushes to support markets; do not bet against the administration.
claims.conditions: poor polls would make it more dangerous

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: The flows will be essentially gone after mid December
claims.claim: After the midterms macro worsens and flows disappear after mid-December, and the administration may allow a controlled crisis to reset.
claims.conditions: assumes they win the Senate; losing it would be worse

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: have an administration that probably wants a bit of a crisis, a controlled crisis, but a crisis.
claims.claim: The administration may want a controlled crisis post-midterm to take markets down and then rally them (take it down to take it up).

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: I would wait till the midterms then I would attack Iran
claims.claim: Karsan reads Trump's likely playbook as waiting until after the midterms and then attacking Iran, with inflationary effects.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: midterm years like which is this year right are historically the worst
claims.claim: Midterm years are historically the weakest for US equities, particularly Q2 and Q3.
claims.indicator: US equity returns in midterm years
claims.direction: equities weak in midterm years Q2-Q3

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: administration doing everything it can to stable the stabilize the ship in the short term because of the midterm
claims.claim: The oil spike did not materialize partly because of positioning and partly because the administration stabilised macro ahead of the midterm; now the oil-up bet is turning more interesting.
claims.direction: long oil as positioning has reversed

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: you did have a little bit of a nice opportunity in oil and kind of uh rates there for for a little bit in the initial inflation but then a very quick controlling of that volatility
claims.claim: The 2026 inflation/oil shock briefly offered long-vol opportunities in oil and rates, but policy quickly controlled and compressed that volatility, cutting the payoff short.
claims.direction: oil and rates vol spike then fast compression
claims.conditions: when authorities act quickly to contain an inflation shock
claims.testable: partly - vol series available, policy attribution is judgement

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: The US can print inordinate amounts of money. And again, that may undermine the exorbitant privilege of the dollar.
claims.claim: The caveat to the money-printing plan is that large-scale monetisation may itself erode the dollar's exorbitant privilege that makes it possible.
claims.conditions: if printing is large enough to undermine confidence

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: China has already been doing this for a decade they just have been doing it buying creating a sovereign wealth fund to do it because they don't operate in the same free market system
claims.claim: Precedent: China has for a decade printed money and channelled it as direct state investment into strategic companies, the model the US is now adapting through a market-based fund.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: they fund 85% of their social welfare through through the summer
claims.claim: Data point offered as evidence: Norway's sovereign wealth fund finances about 85% of its social welfare, showing state equity ownership can replace redistribution.
claims.indicator: Norway SWF share of welfare funding
claims.testable: partly - figure can be checked against Norwegian budget data

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: I think increasingly the US will have more say in these business as well now has a bit of a mandate right to to hire American
claims.claim: Government equity stakes come with growing state say over company decisions (e.g. hiring American), so stake-held firms will partly serve national goals, not only shareholders.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: this will happen for 10 probably 20 years um and start incrementally making progress on these things
claims.claim: The state-ownership and monetisation plan is a 10-20 year programme that only incrementally eases the pressures, not a one-off fix.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: I think that that's that's likely and and there's no uh again as long as there's no in influence.
claims.claim: As part of the trade bargain the US is likely to let China buy more passive stakes in US businesses, with the line drawn at any influence over them.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: working it's forcing strength in the dollar it's forcing more control
claims.claim: The US approach, though barely started, is already working by forcing dollar strength and more control, leaning on incumbent advantages and a more open, more popular system, so success is more likely than not.
claims.conditions: if the plan keeps control; not without risk
claims.testable: partly - dollar index path can be tracked

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: how we're having a really kind of geopolitical kind of um war underneath the surface, and it really is war.
claims.claim: Russia-Ukraine tanker flows and the Venezuela embargo/tanker seizure are linked, making geopolitics a hot rather than purely economic conflict that matters for oil markets.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: what tends to not be as quick moving is actual positioning, cash positioning. It tends to move a little slower.
claims.claim: Survey sentiment moves fast but actual cash and margin positioning is slower and is real money, so positioning data is a more reliable read on crowding than sentiment.
claims.testable: partly - positioning series exist, threshold not given

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: cash positioning is uh for for uh your average investor is at the lowest ever. Um below 3%. And margin uh for investing is also at record highs.
claims.claim: Record-low cash (<3%) plus record margin debt plus record valuations leaves equities fragile, since little buying power remains.
claims.indicator: investor cash allocation; margin debt; valuation
claims.conditions: when cash is lowest ever, margin at record and valuations at record
claims.testable: yes - cash/margin/valuation extremes can be tested vs forward returns

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the VIX measures at-the-money uh implied volatility. And naturally, low the lower the market goes, you slide to a higher implied volatility.
claims.claim: The VIX rises mechanically as the market falls because at-the-money vol slides up the skew, so its rise alone does not show fear.
claims.testable: yes - decompose VIX into skew-slide vs fixed-strike change

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: see how they were moving on implied vol relative to their strike, or in other words, fixed strike vol. That is the the best fear indicator out there.
claims.claim: Fixed-strike implied vol (change in vol of each option holding strike constant) is a better fear and risk indicator than the VIX.
claims.indicator: fixed-strike implied vol of S&P options

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: compression of vol during these quarterly OPEX weeks, the week leading into it and the week of
claims.claim: Around big quarterly (especially year-end) OPEX, structured-product and option positioning compresses vol in the week before and week of expiry.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: it is much more likely to see higher uh prices on a fixed strike basis.
claims.claim: After the OPEX-related supply of vol diminishes, buyers step in and fixed-strike vol is more likely to rise, so the compression is a buying point for vol.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: one of the best trades in when I started in the business in '98, '99, 2000, 2001, 2002 for a four four or five-year period was really to be uh long out-of-the-money uh calls
claims.claim: In the 1998-2002 bubble, long ~25-delta calls three months or more out (stock replacement, even hedged with short stock net long a little delta) beat owning stock because markets rose with vol up.
claims.direction: long OTM calls instead of stock
claims.conditions: bubble regimes with rising vol; not very short-dated options
claims.testable: partly - one episode, needs definition of bubble regime

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the the bigger moves happen at the end. Um, and then eventually it's a bubble and it ends.
claims.claim: Late in a bubble the biggest, fastest moves occur and volatility rises, so the payoff distribution becomes more leptokurtic on both tails.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: why own the whole asset when you can just own the right tail, which is by by the way the cheapest thing in in implied implied vol basis on the curve.
claims.claim: The upside tail (OTM calls) is the cheapest part of the implied vol surface, so owning the right tail is better value than owning the asset when outcomes become leptokurtic.
claims.indicator: OTM call implied vol vs ATM
claims.conditions: when the return distribution is expected to fatten on the right tail

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: The long-term average of at-the-money vol is about a 17 uh vol.
claims.claim: A 25-delta S&P call priced near 12 vol is at a discount to the roughly 17 long-term average ATM vol, which makes it cheap (negative risk premium) in a bubble.
claims.indicator: S&P 25-delta call implied vol vs 17 long-run ATM vol
claims.testable: yes - compare implied vs long-run average

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: we have seen significant support to longer-term vol.
claims.claim: After a fixed-strike implied vol low in August, longer-dated vol found support and the desk saw vol buying opportunities for the next three months.
claims.testable: partly - claim of a past call

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Uh we are definitely playing from the long vol side on the right tail.
claims.claim: Desk view: stay long vol on the right tail and monetize on the 5% pullbacks while implied vol is likely higher into year-end.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: value quality focused over the long term cuz that reduces volatility, even though long-term returns are similar to growth uh things.
claims.claim: Value/quality stocks have lower volatility than growth with similar long-run returns, which improves risk-adjusted return.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: as interest rates go higher, multiple contraction is an issue for equities.
claims.claim: Rising rates compress equity multiples, so equities are hurt by higher rates through valuation.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: interest rates are generally tied to inflation, higher inflation means higher costs, which reduces profit margins.
claims.claim: For most companies margins fall as rates rise because rates track inflation and inflation raises costs.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: There are a sub- subset, about 25%, a significant minority, um that that do the opposite.
claims.claim: About 25% of companies, notably negative-working-capital businesses such as insurers and many financials, see margins improve as rates and inflation rise because they get cash upfront, pay later and face fewer competitors.
claims.indicator: negative working capital; margin sensitivity to rates
claims.testable: yes - sort stocks by working capital and test

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Middleman businesses don't have more costs. Volume goes up, they do well.
claims.claim: Transactional or distributor businesses (card networks, banks, Coca-Cola) benefit in inflation because nominal volumes rise without proportional cost increases.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: a rising long into the curve. And a and importantly, a steepening curve.
claims.claim: Buffett's top holdings (banks, insurers, energy, distributors) are positioned for rising long rates and a steeper yield curve, which is a risk-management play.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: if there's one company that's a major that will benefit, it's Chevron, actually.
claims.claim: Chevron is the major most likely to benefit from Venezuela developments because it has existing Venezuelan operations.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: you can use the brakes to go around the turns, you can accelerate, then you're in control, there's less risk, and you can go faster on average. You can add leverage.
claims.claim: Good risk management (diversification, quality) lets you apply leverage and earn higher returns, rather than just taking less risk.
claims.direction: add leverage to a higher-Sharpe portfolio
claims.testable: yes - compare levered high-Sharpe vs unlevered

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Bonds are not a diversifier to stocks. They do not reduce your risk. It is just a matter of taking the speed down of the portfolio.
claims.claim: 60/40 just lowers total risk and return at the same Sharpe ratio; bonds do not diversify stocks.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: When you when you get to a two Sharpe by diversification or other measures of managing risk, um then you lose use leverage, and that's how you get outsize returns.
claims.claim: Hedge funds first raise Sharpe through diversification and risk control, then use leverage to create outsize returns; without leverage Buffett-like quality only lowers risk.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: because drawdowns are rarer, you have less data on drawdowns and people can have 5 10-year track records with great Sharps, but have tremendous tails of the portfolio.
claims.claim: Drawdowns are rare so a 5-10 year track record with a good Sharpe can hide large tail risk until it hits.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: You really want area under the curve with some measure adjusting for you know amount of size as well.
claims.claim: Prefer a risk measure that penalizes bigger losses (Sortino or area under the drawdown curve) over Sharpe, which treats upside and downside vol alike.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: I think the difference is nowadays the structural flows of buyers versus sellers is just much bigger than it's ever been relative to other flows.
claims.claim: Structural (non-opinion) flows are now larger and more measurable than ever, so understanding market microstructure and positioning gives an edge.
claims.testable: partly - flows are hard to measure fully

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: So understand that positioning, understand the effects that that positioning will have as it is either unwound or as as hedging to those positioning kind of are done.
claims.claim: To anticipate regime shifts, estimate who is positioned and how that positioning will be unwound or hedged; reflexivity arises from these reaction functions.
claims.testable: partly - positioning data coverage is limited

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: those flows generally mean reverting to some some reality and that generally happens as liquidity comes out of the system at some point.
claims.claim: Short-term positioning drives moves for days to 2 years, but over 5-10 years flows mean-revert as liquidity leaves, with timing hard to predict.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: if you can collect that data and have a good sense of what some positioning is or broad positioning. You don't have to know everything.
claims.claim: Rough positioning data plus a model of how holders react is enough; the reaction function is what is solved for.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: that'll tell you then what the reactionary flows should be.
claims.claim: For options, time decay, vol changes and spot moves mechanically produce hedging flows that can be inferred from positioning.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Generally speaking, the reflexive effects on implied volatility are much stronger.
claims.claim: Positioning has stronger effects on implied vol than on the underlying because vol is less liquid, so the path of implied vol is easier to predict from positioning.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: They are important for it for the move, the direction, but they during some periods are significantly smaller and even when they're bigger are maybe 40% at at the best.
claims.claim: Delta flows from option hedging (gamma, vanna, charm) explain at best about 40% of direction and are sometimes much smaller.
claims.testable: yes - regress returns on flow estimates

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: I do think the distributional effects of implied vol compression and the those are much more predictable and much more powerful and easy easy to use.
claims.claim: Predicting the distribution (vol compression/expansion) is more reliable than predicting direction from option flows.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Um you know, we've had this very clear broad thesis about structural inflation and populism, right?
claims.claim: Karsan's structural-inflation and populism thesis led to calls on gold and gold vol (gold at 2500, buy 3000 calls) years ago.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the way it was performing relative to all other commodities was completely out of line with that.
claims.claim: Gold lagged other commodities despite being the best asset for structural inflation, so the gap was a relative-value opportunity in precious metals, not a broad commodities call.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: you want to sell puts in in oil. Uh collect that premium and go plow it into as many long calls in gold as you can.
claims.claim: Sell oil puts and buy gold calls with the premium: a near zero-cost trade that gains convexity to gold while collecting premium in oil.
claims.direction: short oil vol, long gold vol
claims.conditions: structural inflation regime; does not pay every year

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the inflation of the '60s and '70s had four different bouts. It was not one secular move.
claims.claim: Structural inflation comes in cyclical waves, so a long-term inflation view must tolerate months-long inflation lulls.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: During '60s and '70s, precious metals were not only the best performing asset, most people know that, but it was the most volatile asset.
claims.claim: In the 1960s-70s, precious metals were both the best-performing and most volatile asset.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: its implied vol simultaneously at the lows on a risk-adjusted basis, that was one of the most ridiculous trades.
claims.claim: With precious metals vol at lows relative to other assets while the best asset was the most volatile, long gold vol was very cheap.
claims.indicator: gold implied vol vs other assets

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: over that decade 14 years '68 to '82, it went nowhere in nominal terms. So talk about implied vol compression.
claims.claim: Equity index went nowhere nominally from 1968-82, so equity implied vol compressed in that regime.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Uh that FX vol is the way to go. I've been saying it for four or five years.
claims.claim: FX vol (and precious metals, which trade like FX) should be long in the structural inflation regime.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: precious metals, FX, bond vol dramatically higher on all time frames. And then you go look at equity vol. Long-term vol equity dramatically lower.
claims.claim: Regime rule: precious metal, FX and bond vol rise on all horizons, while long-dated equity vol falls (short-term only in line).
claims.direction: long metals/FX/bond vol, short long-dated equity vol

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: multiples should contract cuz as interest rates go higher, multiples need to contract to stay in line with that.
claims.claim: Structurally rising rates and inflation force equity multiples down.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: structurally if you're selling out of the money puts, a much safer play.
claims.claim: Industrial commodities are capped by deglobalization and spiked by inflation, so selling OTM puts (not calls) in energy is safer.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: This is a structural cycle. Uh the populist is populism is, which is a function of inequality.
claims.claim: Populism is the outcome of an inequality cycle, so this is not a sample of one; it provides a structural basis for the 1960s-70s analogy.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: because when you are young, you are labor. And when you retire and you're old, you're capital.
claims.claim: Inequality expansion is felt unequally across generations; young labor is disenfranchised while the old own capital, which drives political change.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: it's not good for predicting one-year, two-year outcomes or five-year outcomes, but if you're looking at 80-year, 40-year, 20-year, decade outcomes, it's incredibly valuable to understand those dynamics.
claims.claim: The inequality/populism cycle is useful for decade-scale outcomes but not for 1-5 year forecasts.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: you want to be able to do things that you measure. Those are the things that are the best for prediction that can give you great conviction.
claims.claim: Base views on measurable structural drivers (generation, inequality, political views) to get conviction.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: inflation is is really the only way out unless you're willing to accept a crisis in these environments.
claims.claim: Since 1971 the Fed is unconstrained by gold, so governments facing political pain choose nominal inflation over market crashes; a flat nominal market hides the loss.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Again, 68 to 82, market dropped at its peak over after a 14-year window and in real terms, um, you know, 60% 55, 60%.
claims.claim: From 1968-82 the equity market fell about 55-60% in real terms yet was flat nominally.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: 60 of those 82 years in decades in in consecutive decades made no money in 60/40 in real terms.
claims.claim: 60/40 delivered zero real return over 1900-1920, 1929-1949 and 1963-1982 (60 of 82 years), so it only worked after rates peaked in 1982.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: 1982 is the peak of interest rates and it went in a diagonal line for 40 years to zero, which created over 400% multiple expansion in equities alone.
claims.claim: 60/40 success since 1982 is an artifact of falling rates that created 400%+ equity multiple expansion.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: we've gone from record low profit margins in 1982 to record high profit margins.
claims.claim: Profit margins are highly correlated with rates and moved from record lows in 1982 to record highs, adding to returns.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: The correlation of stocks and bonds over the long run is more positively correlated than negative.
claims.claim: Over 125 years there was zero diversification benefit between stocks and bonds, and stock-bond correlation is mostly positive.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: And the 80 years that I talked about, those numbers are 0.27 and 0.26. You actually lose your sharp ratio.
claims.claim: Sharpe is ~0.35 for stocks vs 0.37 for 60/40 over 125 years, and 0.27 vs 0.26 over 1900-82, so 60/40 adds nothing.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: And because the sharp ratio for the last 40 years for S&P is 0.52 and 60/40's 0.62, you have gotten some diversification benefit, but that's simply a function of interest rates going down and being used as a tool.
claims.claim: The 60/40 diversification benefit of the last 40 years (Sharpe 0.62 vs 0.52) comes only from falling rates.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: But if we don't know where interest rates are going, it is an incredibly poor way to invest. It's dramatically suboptimal. There is no risk management.
claims.claim: 60/40 is suboptimal without a view on rates and is dangerous if rates rise, unlevered or not.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: The 60-year average 10-year bond is 5.8%.
claims.claim: 10-year yields are still below the 60-year average of 5.8%, so a structural rise in rates is a high-probability scenario.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the steepener is the best trade you can put on
claims.claim: Steepener has been the best rates trade for years, including when the curve was inverted.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: You can achieve risk-adjusted returns, and I am not exaggerating, relatively straightforward with diversification with a little bit of long ball and an and and improving your geometric returns, some value investing like Warren Buffett.
claims.claim: Diversification, a little convexity (long ball), geometric-return focus and value investing give a robust portfolio without needing alpha.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: We're talking about four times the risk-adjusted returns over 125 years.
claims.claim: Simple risk-management concepts could raise a 0.35 Sharpe several-fold; nobody does it because people extrapolate recent history.
claims.testable: partly - claim not backed by shown test

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: people just chase whatever worked the last 5 10 years and 40 years is forever for people.
claims.claim: Investors extrapolate recent performance, so they adopt 60/40 and only change after losses.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: That pool of assets has tripled in 2 years. 2 and 1/2 years.
claims.claim: Non-correlated assets (precious metals, crypto, hedge funds, options-based ETFs/structured products) tripled from ~$5T to ~$15T in 2.5 years as investors seek non-correlation.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: if we are happening to go into a period where interest rates do trend higher and there is but worse returns for assets than we've seen in the last 40 years
claims.claim: If rates trend higher with weaker asset returns for a decade, flows into non-correlated strategies should continue, since most investors only react after losses.
claims.conditions: rates rising with weak asset returns

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: There is an interaction we talked about on here of hedge fund long short equity, which is growing dramatically because of the demand for hedge fund assets.
claims.claim: Growth of long/short hedge funds plus vol compression from structured products and ETFs reflexively changes how underlying assets move.
claims.indicator: hedge fund equity exposure; vol compression

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: There was a a massive part of the structural demand that pushed this market higher was the underweight of equities of institutions having to buy back in
claims.claim: In 2025 institutional underweights forced buying back in and stable vol compression allowed risk-taking and helped policymakers after Liberation Day.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: we thought it'd be a 15-ish percent type decline and then a rally.
claims.claim: The desk called the Feb-April 2025 drop (15% expected, 25% actual), bought the dip and was aggressive on the rally.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Whereas last 40 it's average is 7.1 years. Um that is because of this populist um impulse and and the political upheaval that's coming as a result of it.
claims.claim: In populist periods presidential turnover is faster (5 presidents in 1962-82, about 4 years each vs 7.1 years average in the last 40), reflecting political upheaval.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Just wait. The pitchforks are going to be on his lawn. Give it 6 to 9 months.
claims.claim: Karsan predicted that exuberance after Trump's election would fade within 6-9 months, with approval falling and the base moving away.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Presidential elections during that '62 to '82 period, we have five of them. All five are double-digit positive with an average return of 21 and 1/2%.
claims.claim: In populist periods (1962-82) all five presidential election years returned double digits (average 21.5%).

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: If you take out that five out of the 25 for 100 years the average return is closer to six, seven which is meaningfully under the long-term average.
claims.claim: Excluding the 1962-82 populist years, presidential election years average only 6-7%, below the long-term average, so the election-year effect is specific to populist regimes.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the other 15 years combined have an average uh nominal performance uh of of negative 3%.
claims.claim: Non-election years in 1962-82 averaged -3% nominal.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: You know what the return is at the presidential election into 2020? Or in 2020? 18 and 1/2%.
claims.claim: 2020 (+18.5%) and 2024 (+25%) election years fit the populist-period election pattern.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: we didn't go mining data to find this. We had this big qualitative idea, we went looked at data, and it screams at you.
claims.claim: Theory-first, data-second (not data mining) is the speaker's argument for the election-year findings.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: So, if you go look at '62, '66, '70, '74. Okay. All of them um were massive down years.
claims.claim: Midterm years of the populist period (1962, 66, 70, 74) were all large down years, especially over the 15 months starting in Q3 of the year before.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the biggest drawdown of those four is 42%.
claims.claim: Midterm drawdowns in populist periods reach as much as 42%, start earlier and get bigger over time.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: by the middle of the midterm year he was in price controls as inflation picked up.
claims.claim: Nixon cut taxes first, then by the midterm year had price controls amid inflation; today fiscal spending is likely to return as pitchforks show up.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: And those pressures are the problem ultimately for equity markets.
claims.claim: Political pressure from populism is the ultimate problem for equities, and for bonds too.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: a very stable rally, a lot of vol compression in the summer driven by structural factors. [L120] Um, that was a natural buying point in vol.
claims.claim: A stable rally with structurally driven summer vol compression (as before 1998-99) is a natural point to buy volatility, since bubble endings bring bigger two-way moves.
claims.indicator: implied vol level after a structurally compressed stable rally
claims.conditions: late-stage bubble with structural (product-driven) vol compression
claims.testable: partly - vol compression measurable, bubble label subjective

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Everybody likes to think about direction specifically in the effects of the options and they started with gamma. I've added vol and charm. People have largely now absorbed that in the last four or five years
claims.claim: Directional option-hedging flow analysis (gamma, then vanna and charm) has been widely absorbed over the last 4-5 years, so the remaining edge is in the less-watched distributional effects of implied vol.
claims.conditions: edge decays as the method spreads
claims.testable: partly - could compare predictive power before/after ~2020

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: like the volma and beta, these effects that are that are tied to the vol have effects on the distribution of the underlying. But they're not necessarily the delta effects.
claims.claim: Second-order vol-linked option effects (volga/vanna-type) move the distribution of the underlying rather than its direction.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: if you just knew that interest rates were going top left to bottom right for 40 years which is what happened for 40 years. If that if you understood that one dynamic one thing
claims.claim: One secular driver (the 40-year fall in interest rates) drove nearly all asset returns, so getting the single regime driver right matters more than short-term direction calls.
claims.indicator: secular trend in long-term interest rates
claims.testable: partly - return attribution to rates is measurable

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: hard to predict direction. General dynamics apply, but predicting distribution given some very basic assumptions can be uh can be very predictable.
claims.claim: In a regime, the relative distribution of volatility across assets is far more predictable from basic assumptions than price direction, allowing decade-long vol calls.
claims.indicator: cross-asset implied vs realized vol by regime

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: you could see outcomes that are not as inflationary, that could become deflationary ultimately as a function breakdown.
claims.claim: Caveat: the inequality/populism cycle can also end in a deflationary breakdown rather than inflation; the 1960s-70s inflationary analog applies because post-1971 the Fed can inflate.
claims.conditions: inflationary outcome needs an unconstrained central bank (fiat since 1971)

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: And this is why markets are going up and I even though interest rates went up in 20, you know, to 4 and 1/2 relatively in the last year or so, uh more stable, right?
claims.claim: The tripling of money in non-correlated strategies and option-based products is why markets rose and stayed relatively stable despite rates rising to about 4.5%.
claims.indicator: AUM in non-correlated assets (precious metals, crypto, hedge funds, option ETFs/structured products)
claims.direction: equities up, realized vol down while inflows continue
claims.conditions: while inflows into non-correlated strategies continue
claims.testable: partly - AUM series exist; attribution hard

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: And then lastly, now let's look forward into midterms.
claims.claim: Applying the populist-period midterm pattern forward, the 2026 midterm year (15-month window from about Q3/October 2025) carries elevated risk of a large equity drawdown.
claims.indicator: US midterm election cycle in populist regimes
claims.conditions: populist regime; pattern may be front-run so drawdowns start earlier

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: it's it's unavoidable in a sense un- unless we head to pure authoritarianism and circumvent the whole system, which is possible.
claims.claim: The populist political pressure on markets is unavoidable unless the democratic system is circumvented by authoritarianism, which is the stated exception to the thesis.
claims.conditions: fails if democratic mechanism is bypassed
